155.title: Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom day
155.hook: remembered each year, he is often called the shield of India
155.howItsDone: Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom each year in late autumn with kirtan, readings and langar; many visit Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, where he was executed, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj, where his body was cremated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shaheedi Jor Mela, and two small boys at Sirhind. Your line was small, and unbending. Did you catch a child being brave? Day one hundred fifty-five.

Imagine a group of strangers arriving at your door. They aren't your people. They don't share your faith. They've traveled a long way, and they're frightened. They tell you: our families are being pressured to give up our religion, and we don't know who else to ask. What would you say? Sikhs remember that this is what happened at Anandpur in 1675. The visitors were Kashmiri Pandits, Hindu scholars and priests. And the man they came to see was the ninth Guru.
screen: `STRANGERS AT THE DOOR.` → `NOT YOUR FAITH, NOT YOUR PEOPLE.` → `WHAT WOULD YOU SAY?`

segments.voice: Guru Tegh Bahadur listened. Tradition says he sat quiet a long time and then said it would take the sacrifice of a great soul. His son Gobind, about nine years old, answered: who could be greater than you? So the Guru sent the Pandits back with a message for the officials of the emperor Aurangzeb: if Tegh Bahadur can be made to change his faith, we will all change ours. Then he set out for Delhi himself. He was arrested. Three of his companions, Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, were put to death in front of him, tradition says, to break him. He didn't break. In November 1675, in the square at Chandni Chowk in Delhi, he was beheaded. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands on the spot now. What Sikhs hold on to is this: he gave his life for other people's right to worship, a right he didn't need for himself. He didn't wear their sacred thread or their forehead mark. His son, Guru Gobind Singh, later wrote that his father protected their tilak and their thread, and gave his head but not his faith. That's why he is called Hind di Chadar. Hind is India. A chadar is a sheet, a covering, the cloth you'd put over someone to shelter them. The covering of India. His own verses in the Guru Granth Sahib say, in paraphrase, that the wise one frightens no one and is afraid of no one. Sikhs mark his martyrdom every year, in late autumn, with kirtan, and many visit Sis Ganj.
screen: `A PLEA FROM KASHMIR.` · `WHO COULD BE GREATER THAN YOU?` · `CHANDNI CHOWK, 1675.` · `CHADAR — A SHELTERING CLOTH.` · then, large: `HIND DI CHADAR.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and think of people anywhere in the world who can't practice their faith freely, or who are pushed to take on one they don't hold. You don't have to name a country. Let them be people: a family at dinner, a grandmother, a kid at school who hides what she believes. If you pray, you can pray for their freedom, in your own words or simply with Waheguru. If you don't pray, wish them room to believe as they choose, and to be left in peace. The bell holds the time.
Hind di Chadar. The covering of India: a name for Guru Tegh Bahadur, who gave his life so others could keep their faith.
Your line: a shield for others. Today, stand up for someone's right to be who they are, even in a small way: a joke you don't laugh at, a name you learn to say correctly. Day one hundred fifty-five.

156.title: Camp 3 close: your rhythm
156.hook: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, a bani and a visit: now assemble a week
156.howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep a daily Nitnem of set prayers at dawn, dusk and night, do simran, and go to the gurdwara weekly for kirtan, langar and seva; the rhythm grows over years rather than all at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Hind di Chadar. Your line was a shield for others. Did you get a chance to stand beside someone, even in a small way? Day one hundred fifty-six.
screen: `HIND DI CHADAR — A SHIELD FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Sixty days ago, this camp started with shoes. Tidying the shoes by your door, as seva. Since then you've listened to kirtan, eaten sitting on the floor in a row, breathed the Name, learned the daily prayers, and walked, in your mind at least, into a gurdwara. Then a whole year of festivals, from Vaisakhi to yesterday. That's a lot of practices, and nobody does all of them every day. So today isn't a new practice. Today it's you, with a pen, building a week.
screen: `IT STARTED WITH SHOES.` → `SIXTY DAYS OF PRACTICES.` → `NOW, BUILD A WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's what this camp gave you, in six parts. Seva: nishkam seva, service with no audience, and daswandh, a tenth for others, and a warning about haumai, the ego that loves credit. Kirtan: raag, the mood; rahao, the pause; the sangat singing back. Langar: pangat, the same row on the floor. Simran: the Name on the breath, the amrit vela before dawn, the mala, bead by bead. The banis: Nitnem, from Japji at dawn to Rehras at dusk and Sohila at night. And the visit: the Nishan Sahib outside, matha tekna, the chaur, karah prashad, the hukamnama. Then the Sikh year: Vaisakhi, nagar kirtan, gurpurabs, akhand path, chhabeel, Bandi Chhor, Hola Mohalla, Maghi, the Shaheedi Jor Mela, Hind di Chadar. Sikhs have a word for a daily rule, and you've met it: Nitnem. Nit means daily. Nem is a rule, a discipline you keep. The Gurus didn't treat faith as a mood that comes and goes. They built it into the day: early morning, evening, night. And into the week: the gurdwara, the langar, the sangat. A rhythm holds you on the days motivation doesn't. It isn't a test. A small rhythm you keep will carry you further than a big one you drop by Thursday. For many Sikhs the rhythm is Nitnem every day and the gurdwara every week. For a learner or a partner it might be one bani, one meal shared, one quiet morning. Tomorrow a new camp begins: the text itself. Japji Sahib, line by line, starting with its alphabet.
screen: `SEVA, KIRTAN, LANGAR.` · `SIMRAN, THE BANIS, THE VISIT.` · `NITNEM — A DAILY RULE.` · `SMALL AND KEPT.` · then, large: `YOUR RHYTHM.`

segments.voice: Find a pen, or open a note on your phone. Write seven short lines, one for each day of the week. On each line put one small thing from this camp: a bani, five minutes of simran, an unseen seva, one shabad, a meal shared. If a gurdwara is near, give it one day. Keep every line small enough that a bad day could still manage it. If you pray, you might write Waheguru at the top. Then read your seven lines back once, slowly. The bell holds the time.
Camp three, closed. Your word for today is your own rhythm: a Nitnem, a daily rule, sized to your life.
Your line: you can do this. Put your seven lines somewhere you'll see them tomorrow morning, and do the first one. Camp three is done. Day one hundred fifty-six.

157.title: The Guru's alphabet
157.hook: Gurmukhi, from the Guru's mouth, has thirty-five letters and a set of vowel signs
157.howItsDone: Sikh children often learn the Gurmukhi letters at gurdwara Punjabi classes, reciting the painti aloud, so that they can read Gurbani for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp three closed, and you wrote seven small lines. Your line was you can do this. Did the first line of your rhythm happen this morning? Day one hundred fifty-seven.

Think of the first letters you ever learned. Maybe plastic magnets on a fridge. A for apple, B for ball. Before you could read a single word, you could make the sounds, and you were proud of them. Today a new camp begins, and it begins the same way, with letters. For the next seventy-five days we'll read one text together, slowly: Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib, the first hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib. To do that, it helps to meet the script it's written in.
screen: `MAGNETS ON THE FRIDGE.` → `A NEW CAMP: THE TEXT.` → `JAPJI SAHIB, LINE BY LINE.`

segments.voice: The script is Gurmukhi. Gur is Guru. Mukhi comes from mukh, the mouth. From the mouth of the Guru. Sikhs trace it to Guru Angad, the second Guru, who, tradition says, shaped and settled the letters so the Sikhs could write down Guru Nanak's hymns. The letters grew out of older scripts already used in Punjab; Guru Angad gave them a form, and a purpose. The alphabet is called the painti, which simply means thirty-five, because it has thirty-five basic letters. It opens with three letters that carry vowels, oora, aira and eeree, and then the consonants march in neat rows: sassa, haha, then kakka, khakha, gagga, and on. Around the letters sit a set of vowel signs, small marks above, below and beside them, that change the sound. Later, a handful of extra letters with a dot at the foot were added for sounds borrowed from Persian, so modern charts show a few more than thirty-five. Here's the gift for a learner: Gurmukhi is close to phonetic. Mostly, you say what you see. So you can sound out Japji long before you understand it, the way a child sings a song before knowing what the words mean. And the very first character of the Guru Granth Sahib isn't a letter at all. It's the numeral one, joined to the letter oora, with a long curve sweeping over the top: Ik Onkar. The One, who is everywhere. The whole scripture begins with a number and a sound. So in this camp, we read with the mouth first. Understanding follows.
screen: `GURMUKHI — FROM THE GURU'S MOUTH.` · `GURU ANGAD SETTLES THE LETTERS.` · `THE PAINTI — THIRTY-FIVE.` · `SAY WHAT YOU SEE.` · then, large: `IK ONKAR.`

segments.voice: Look at the symbol on the screen: Ik Onkar. Lift one finger, and trace it in the air, slowly, as if you're writing on a window. First the numeral one. Then the round letter beside it. Then the long curve that sweeps up over the top and keeps going. Do it three times, a little smoother each time. Then rest your hand in your lap, breathe, and let the shape stay behind your eyes. If you pray, you can say Ik Onkar quietly as you trace. The bell holds the time.
Gurmukhi. From the Guru's mouth: the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, with thirty-five letters and a set of vowel signs.
Your line: read with the mouth first. Today, find Gurmukhi somewhere, a sign, a food label, a screen, and try saying one letter out loud. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

158.title: Sound before meaning
158.hook: Japji is meant to be heard; we will listen to each pauri before we learn what it says
158.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite or listen to Japji Sahib every morning, often from memory, as the first bani of Nitnem; children usually learn it by hearing it long before they study its meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi, the script from the Guru's mouth. Your line was read with the mouth first. Did you find a Gurmukhi letter out in the world and say it? Day one hundred fifty-eight.

Think of a song in a language you don't speak that still gets to you. A lullaby a grandmother sang. A chant in a stadium. A hymn at a wedding where you caught maybe one word in ten. The meaning never reached you. The sound did, and it stayed. Sikhs have long known this about Japji. Before most Sikh children know what it says, they know how it sounds, because they've heard it at dawn, drifting from a kitchen or a car radio, for as long as they can remember.
screen: `A SONG YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND.` → `THE SOUND STAYED.` → `JAPJI AT DAWN, FROM THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: So this camp has a rule. Almost every pauri, every stanza, gets two days. The first day is sound: we listen, and say the opening line out loud. The second day is meaning: what the Guru is saying. Sound first, then meaning. Why that order? Partly because of what Japji is. The name comes from jap, to recite, to repeat. It was made to be said, not only studied. Many Sikhs recite it every morning as the first prayer of Nitnem, often from memory. It has thirty-eight pauris, with a short salok at the start and another at the end, and a steady recitation takes around twenty minutes. Partly it's because of how Gurbani, the Guru's word, speaks about itself. The hymns keep praising the shabad, the word as sound, and the naad, the sound that moves through everything, as things that work on the one who hears them. Japji itself will give four whole pauris to one word: suniai, by listening. We'll get there. And partly it's simply how learning works. Understanding goes deeper when it lands on something already familiar. If you've said a line thirty times, then on the day its meaning arrives, it has somewhere to sit. There's a humility in it, too. You don't have to understand everything before you start. You're allowed to listen first. When we do open the meanings, we'll follow Macauliffe's 1909 translation, retold in plain words. But for now, the instruction is short. Listen.
screen: `TWO DAYS FOR EACH PAURI.` · `JAPJI IS MADE TO BE SAID.` · `THE SHABAD WORKS ON THE LISTENER.` · `LISTEN FIRST, UNDERSTAND LATER.` · then, large: `SOUND BEFORE MEANING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice starts now and finishes later. Now: close your eyes, and just listen to whatever is around you, the hum of a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Don't name the sounds. Just hear them. Later today, find a recording of Japji Sahib, there are many, and let it play once, all the way through, while you cook or drive or walk. Don't follow the words. Don't look anything up. Let it wash past. If you pray, you can simply sit inside it. The bell holds the time.
Sound before meaning. In this camp, each pauri of Japji is heard and said before it is explained.
Your line: listen before you understand. Play Japji once today, start to finish, and notice one sound that stays with you afterward. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

159.title: The Mool Mantar, sounded
159.hook: Ik Onkar, Satnam, Karta Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akal Murat, Ajuni, Saibhang, Gur Prasad
159.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji each morning and at many other moments; a short form, Ik Onkar Satgur Prasad, stands at the head of hymns throughout the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sound before meaning. Your line was listen before you understand. Did Japji play once, all the way through, and did one sound stay with you? Day one hundred fifty-nine.

Every community has a line people know by heart. The words that come out without thinking, at a wedding, a funeral, a bedside. Sikhs have one that comes before everything else. It opens the Guru Granth Sahib. It opens Japji. A short form of it stands at the head of hymns all through the scripture. Many Sikh children can say it before they can read it. It's called the Mool Mantar, the root verse. Today we don't explain it. We just learn how it sounds.
screen: `A LINE EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `IT OPENS THE WHOLE GRANTH.` → `TODAY, ONLY THE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Mool means root. Mantar is a verse to be repeated. The root verse. Here it is, slowly, in its pieces. Ik Onkar. Ik, like ick; Onkar, ong-KAAR. Sat Naam. Sat, rhyming with but; naam, like calm with an n. Kartaa Purakh. KAR-taa, PUR-akh. Nirbhau. nir-BHOW, like now, with a breath on the b. Nirvair. nir-VAIR, like air. Akaal Moorat. a-KAAL, MOO-rat. Ajoonee. a-JOO-nee. Saibhang. say-BHUNG. Gur Prasaad. gur pra-SAAD. That's the whole thing: about a dozen words. Say it slowly and it takes fifteen seconds. You've already half-heard their outline, and we'll keep meeting them all through Japji: one; truth is the name; the maker; without fear; without hate; beyond time; unborn; self-existent; known by the Guru's grace. Now notice the sound itself. It moves in short beats, two and three syllables at a time, easy to breathe with. Its first sound is a number: ik, one. Its middle is a run of nirs and a's, nirbhau, nirvair, akaal, ajoonee, each one saying what the One is not: not afraid, not hating, not bound by time, not born. And the last two words, gur prasaad, turn the whole verse into a gift: this isn't something you figure out, it's something given. Sikhs differ a little on where the Mool Mantar ends. Many end it at gur prasaad. Others carry on through the next lines, to Nanak hosee bhee sach. Both are said with love, every morning.
screen: `MOOL — ROOT. MANTAR — VERSE.` · `SHORT BEATS, EASY TO BREATHE.` · `IT STARTS WITH A NUMBER.` · `GUR PRASAAD — A GIFT.` · then, large: `THE MOOL MANTAR.`

segments.voice: Now it's yours. Sit up, breathe in, and say it slowly, out loud if you can, in a whisper if you can't. Ik Onkar. Sat Naam. Kartaa Purakh. Nirbhau. Nirvair. Akaal Moorat. Ajoonee. Saibhang. Gur Prasaad. Take a breath between each piece. Then say it once more, a little smoother. Don't worry about every vowel; say what you heard. If you pray, it's already a prayer. If you're learning, it's a sound worth knowing by heart. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ`

segments.voice: The Mool Mantar. The root verse that opens the Guru Granth Sahib, from Ik Onkar to Gur Prasaad.
Your line: sound it out. Say the Mool Mantar once more before you sleep tonight, slowly, from Ik Onkar to Gur Prasaad. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

160.title: The title word
160.hook: after the Mool Mantar comes one word, jap: recite, repeat, remember
160.howItsDone: Japji Sahib takes its name from jap, to recite and remember; Sikhs recite it each morning, and many also repeat Waheguru or the Mool Mantar through the day as simran.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mool Mantar, from Ik Onkar to Gur Prasaad. Your line was sound it out. Did you say it once more before sleep? Day one hundred sixty.

Think of the notes you leave yourself. Not whole sentences. One word on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror: call. Milk. Breathe. One word, because one word is all you need to remember by. Right after the Mool Mantar, before the first verse of Japji begins, there's a single word standing on its own line. Most people read straight past it. It's the title of the whole hymn. And it isn't really a name, the way a book title is. It's closer to a note on the mirror.
screen: `A STICKY NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `ONE WORD, ON ITS OWN LINE.` → `A TITLE LIKE A NOTE.`

segments.voice: The word is jap. In Gurmukhi it's just two letters, with a small vowel mark under the second that carries grammar and is mostly left silent. You've met its meaning before, folded inside a longer name: on day twenty-one and again on day one hundred twenty-nine, Japji Sahib, the recitation, with ji and sahib added for respect. Today, look at the word with the respect taken off, standing alone on its line. Across Indian religious life there's a practice called japa: repeating a sacred name or phrase, often on beads. You met the mala in camp three. Jap comes from the same root. So the bare title of Guru Nanak's great morning hymn reads like one instruction: repeat. Or: remember. But here's the thing Japji itself will teach. It isn't asking for mechanical repetition. Much later in the hymn, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that if one tongue became a hundred thousand, and each repeated the Name a hundred thousand times, those would be the steps of a stairway toward the Lord. Repetition is a stairway. And yet the whole hymn insists the point is remembering, not counting: keeping the One in mind while you live. That's why jap sits so close to simran, remembrance, from camp three. Say something enough times and it stops being something you say and becomes something you know in your bones. It's how you learned your own phone number, a friend's laugh, the way home in the dark. Jap asks for that kind of knowing. The stairway is made of small repetitions. Each one is only one step.
screen: `A ONE-WORD TITLE.` · `JAP — RECITE, REPEAT, REMEMBER.` · `THE TITLE, WITH THE RESPECT TAKEN OFF.` · `REPETITION IS A STAIRWAY.` · then, large: `JAP.`

segments.voice: Sit easily. On your next out-breath, whisper the word: jap. Breathe in. Out-breath: jap. Breathe in. Out-breath: jap. Three times. Then stop, and listen to the quiet after it, the way a room sounds after a bell. Notice what you'd like to remember today: a person, a promise, the One, if that's your language. If you pray, you can let Waheguru follow on the next breaths. Rest there for the rest of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Jap. Recite, repeat, remember: the one-word title of Guru Nanak's morning hymn.
Your line: repeat, remember. Pick one good thing to repeat today, a word, a kindness, a slow breath, and do it three times on purpose. Day one hundred sixty.

161.title: Aad sach: the sound
161.hook: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhi sach, Nanak hosi bhi sach
161.howItsDone: The salok 'aad sach, jugaad sach' follows the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji; sangats also sing it as simple kirtan, repeating it many times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jap, the one-word title: recite, repeat, remember. Your line was repeat, remember. What did you repeat three times on purpose? Day one hundred sixty-one.

Right after the title, jap, comes a short verse, a salok, just two lines long. It's one of the most sung lines in the Sikh world. You'll hear it at the start of Japji every morning, and you'll hear it at gatherings as kirtan, sung round and round until the whole room is singing. It has a shape you can feel before you know a single word: four little claims, with the same word landing at the end of each one. Like a drum hitting the same beat four times.
screen: `A SALOK, TWO LINES LONG.` → `SUNG ROUND AND ROUND.` → `ONE WORD, FOUR TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here it is, slowly. Aad sach. Jugaad sach. Hai bhee sach. Naanak hosee bhee sach. Listen for the word that keeps coming back: sach. It sounds a little like such, said softly. That's the drumbeat. Now the pieces. Aad: a long a, as in father. Jugaad: ju-GAAD, and inside it is the word jug, an age, a great stretch of time. Hai bhee: hai, like high, and bhee, like bee with a breath on the b. Naanak: the Guru's own name, NAA-nak. Hosee bhee: HO-see bhee. Now notice the shape. The first line is two short pairs: aad sach, jugaad sach. The second line stretches out: three beats, then four. As if the verse leans forward. And listen to what the pieces sound like even before you know them: aad, a beginning; jug, the ages; hai, is; hosee, will be. It moves from before, through the long ages, to right now, and on into what's coming. And in every line, the same word holds still while the time around it moves. The sound is already doing the teaching before the meaning arrives. Tomorrow we'll open what sach means and what the four lines claim. Today it's enough to hear one word holding the whole verse up. In Gurmukhi, sach carries the same small silent mark under its last letter that you saw on jap. Many sangats sing this salok as simple kirtan, and it's one of the easiest to join.
screen: `SACH — THE DRUMBEAT.` · `AAD, JUGAAD, HAI BHEE, HOSEE.` · `THE SECOND LINE STRETCHES.` · `ONE WORD HOLDS STILL.` · then, large: `AAD SACH.`

segments.voice: Say it four times, out loud if you can. Aad sach. Jugaad sach. Hai bhee sach. Naanak hosee bhee sach. Again, a little slower, letting sach land each time. Again, softer. And once more, almost a whisper. Then sit, and let the last sach fade. Notice that your breath went on the whole time, underneath the words. If you pray, you can stay with Waheguru in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ਆਦਿ ਸਚੁ ਜੁਗਾਦਿ ਸਚੁ ॥ ਹੈ ਭੀ ਸਚੁ ਨਾਨਕ ਹੋਸੀ ਭੀ ਸਚੁ ॥`

segments.voice: Aad sach. The opening words of the salok after the Mool Mantar. One word, sach, holds the whole verse up.

Your line: aad sach. Say it once as you wake tomorrow. And look back at this week: a shield for others, your rhythm, the Guru's alphabet, sound before meaning, the Mool Mantar, and jap. Day one hundred sixty-one.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the salok after the Mool Mantar, Ang 1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chant.
what it means: a two-line salok in which one word, sach, lands four times across past, ages, now and future.
what a scholar hears: jugaad joins jug, an age, to aad, beginning; the verse also closes the Mool Mantar for those who read it as longer.
